meaning: 'Green willow' (Aoyagi and Seiryu are alternative readings of the same characters): the willow that yields and springs back, an image chosen for a kata designed around a woman's build and self-defence needs.
name: Aoyagi
note: Commissioned as a women's self-defence form (taught among others to female railway employees), it blends Shito-ryu and Shindo Jinen-ryu technique with aikido-informed adjustments suggested by Ueshiba. Practised as Aoyagi in Shito-ryu lines and as Seiryu in Konishi's Shindo Jinen-ryu.
origin_person: Kenwa Mabuni and Yasuhiro Konishi, with advice from Morihei Ueshiba
variants: Seiryū (alternative reading of the same kanji)

era: Wado version 1930s (declared among the nine official kata, 1977)
meaning: Named, per established folklore, after the stranded Chinese sailor Chinto whose fighting methods Matsumura recorded; Otsuka kept the Okinawan name where Funakoshi had substituted Gankaku.
name: Chinto (Wado-ryu)
note: Otsuka's Chinto keeps the straight-line embusen and crane stances but re-engineers the form around Wado principles of evasion and body-shifting rather than Shotokan's deep power line, making it the most advanced of the nine official Wado kata.
origin_person: attributed to Sokon Matsumura (folklore); Wado adaptation by Hironori Otsuka

meaning: 'Flying swallow': named for the kata's swift rising and dropping movements and darting changes of level, likened to a swallow in flight.
name: Empi
note: Funakoshi's Japanese rename of the Tomari kata Wanshu, traditionally (folklore) traced to the 1683 Chinese sapposhi Wang Ji. The Shotokan version follows the Itosu line of the kata and was further polished during the 1930s-40s reforms associated with Gigo Funakoshi.
origin_person: Tomari-te lineage attributed to the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (Wanshu); renamed by Gichin Funakoshi
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; renamed in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Crane on a rock': named for the repeated one-legged (crane) stance from which the kata strikes, replacing the untranslatable Chinese-derived name Chinto.
name: Gankaku
note: Funakoshi's rename of Chinto; the Shotokan version, with its rotated embusen, descends through Itosu. The tale of the sailor-pirate Chinto teaching Matsumura in exchange for clemency is established folklore rather than documented history.
origin_person: attributed to Sokon Matsumura from the teachings of the shipwrecked Chinese sailor Chinto (folklore); renamed by Gichin Funakoshi
origin_place: Tomari/Shuri, Okinawa; renamed in Tokyo, Japan

era: renamed 1935 (Seisan among the oldest kata on Okinawa)
meaning: 'Half moon': named for the crescent-shaped stepping and the inward-tensed hangetsu-dachi stance that replaces the Okinawan seisan-dachi; the old name Seisan means 'thirteen'.
name: Hangetsu
note: Shotokan's only breathing-and-tension kata, Funakoshi's rename of the Shuri-te version of Seisan, probably the oldest kata name recorded on Okinawa. The rename is the clearest example of Funakoshi substituting a descriptive Japanese image for a Chinese numeric name.
origin_person: old Okinawan/Chinese lineage (creator unknown); renamed by Gichin Funakoshi
origin_place: Okinawa (Fujian roots); renamed in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Peace and tranquillity' (the on'yomi reading of the same characters as Pinan): Funakoshi glossed it as the confidence of one who, having mastered these forms, can defend himself calmly anywhere.
name: Heian
note: Part of Funakoshi's 1930s programme of replacing Okinawan and Chinese-sounding kata names with Japanese ones, to make karate acceptable to nationalist mainland Japan and to the Dai Nippon Butokukai. Funakoshi also swapped the order of the first two forms, so Shotokan's Heian Shodan corresponds to Itosu's Pinan Nidan.
origin_person: Anko Itosu (created the Pinan series); Gichin Funakoshi (Japanese renaming)
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; renamed in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Ordered path' or 'following the route in sequence': five kata forming a graded route through Asai's body-dynamics method of relaxation, whip-like snap and rotational power.
name: Junro
note: The core of the roughly dozen kata Asai created for his JKS curriculum after leaving the JKA, designed to reintroduce whipping, one-legged and rotational actions he felt standard Shotokan had lost; they are now examined kata within JKS worldwide. (Note: Junro is Asai Shotokan, not an Ashihara or Enshin form.)
origin_place: Tokyo, Japan (Japan Karate Shoto Federation, JKS)

meaning: 'Fundamental paired forms': ten prearranged two-person sequences that Otsuka regarded as kata in their own right, encoding Wado's core principles of nagasu (flowing), inasu (evading) and noru (riding) an attack.
name: Kihon Kumite (Wado-ryu)
note: Otsuka fused Shindo Yoshin-ryu jujutsu pairwork with karate striking to create these paired kata, the most distinctive Japanese-created element of the Wado syllabus and the clearest expression of the style's jujutsu inheritance. They sit alongside, not below, the solo kata in Wado pedagogy.

meaning: Kyoku is usually rendered 'ultimate' or 'reach the limit'; the seven forms progress from very basic technique to long, complex black-belt forms expressing the fighting method of the Shudokan school.
name: Kyoku series
note: The signature Japanese-created kata set of Toyama Kanken's Shudokan (the roster lists him under his Okinawan birth name Oyadomari), originally treated as in-house forms and still taught mainly at brown and black belt; the school also created the meditative forms Soshin, Kakushin and Choshin. Precise authorship within the dojo is not fully documented, so attribution to Toyama personally should be t
origin_person: Kanken Toyama and senior students of the Shudokan

meaning: 'Wind in the pines': Mabuni's poetic rename of the Tomari-te kata Wankan ('king's crown'), evoking calm resilience.
name: Matsukaze
note: Mabuni preserved the fuller Tomari Wankan within Shito-ryu but gave it a Japanese literary name, paralleling Funakoshi's renaming programme; the truncated Shotokan Wankan of Gigo Funakoshi is its cognate. The rename is documented in Shito-ryu organisational kata lists.
origin_person: Tomari-te lineage (Matsumora line); renamed and arranged by Kenwa Mabuni
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; renamed in Osaka, Japan

meaning: 'Bright (polished) mirror': named for the opening movements likened to smoothing the surface of a mirror, and often linked to the sacred mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave in Shinto myth (a symbolic gloss, not documented intent).
name: Meikyo
note: Funakoshi's rename of Rohai ('vision of a heron'); the Shotokan form condenses Itosu's three Rohai into one kata, a reworking generally associated with Gigo Funakoshi, and includes the distinctive sankaku-tobi triangular jump. Tetsuhiko Asai later added Meikyo Nidan and Sandan in his JKS lineage.
origin_person: Rohai lineage from Tomari-te (Matsumora line), arranged by Anko Itosu; renamed and reworked for Shotokan
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; renamed in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Thirteen' (hands or steps), the old Okinawan numeric name, which Otsuka retained rather than adopting Funakoshi's rename Hangetsu.
name: Seishan (Wado-ryu)
note: One of the nine kata Otsuka declared official for Wado-ryu in 1977; he stripped out Okinawan dynamic tension and rooted stances, refitting the kata with Wado's fluid seishan-dachi, taisabaki and the body dynamics of his Shindo Yoshin-ryu jujutsu. He learned the base forms from Funakoshi and refined them through study with Motobu Choki and Mabuni.
origin_person: old Okinawan lineage; Wado adaptation by Hironori Otsuka

meaning: 'Salute to the four directions': by Chito-ryu tradition the bowing sequence derives from ceremonies of the Ryukyuan royal court in which obeisance was made to all four quarters (this courtly origin is folklore).
name: Shihohai
note: The opening kata of Chito-ryu and effectively unique to it, making it a de facto Chitose standardisation whatever its Okinawan source; his own book credits Hanashiro Chomo at Sogen-ji, while some lineage accounts point to Aragaki. The royal-ceremony narrative is transmitted tradition, flagged as such.
origin_person: disputed: learned by Tsuyoshi Chitose from Hanashiro Chomo (per Chitose's Kempo Karate-do) or from Aragaki Seisho
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; preserved in Kumamoto, Japan

meaning: 'Tranquil strength' or 'preserve the peace': strength held in stillness, expressed through the rooted sochin-dachi (fudo-dachi), the 'immovable stance' that dominates the kata.
name: Sochin (Shotokan)
note: The Shotokan Sochin differs so extensively from Aragaki Seisho's Naha/Tomari Sochin (kept in Shito-ryu) that it is treated as Gigo Funakoshi's creation, exemplifying his deep-stance, powerful reform of Shotokan. Gichin Funakoshi's proposed Japanese rename Hakko never displaced the old name.
origin_person: Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi, reworking the Aragaki-line Sochin

meaning: 'Grand ultimate' or 'first cause', from the Chinese taiji: the kata embodies the beginner's mind, and Funakoshi wrote that the advanced student should return to it once mastery is achieved.
name: Taikyoku
note: A set of three (in some lineages six) elementary kata built from a simple I-shaped embusen, published under Gichin Funakoshi's name but widely credited in Shotokan scholarship to Gigo Funakoshi's late-1930s reforms. It spread far beyond Shotokan, seeding the Kyokushin Taikyoku and early taekwondo Kicho forms.
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi with his son Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi

meaning: 'Iron horseman' or 'iron horse riding': named for the kata's rooted horse-riding stance (kiba-dachi), and, by Nakayama's account, in homage to the power of Funakoshi's teacher Itosu, who shaped the form.
name: Tekki
note: Funakoshi's Japanese rename of Naihanchi, the sideways-fighting kata he himself spent roughly ten years studying under Azato and Itosu. The lateral straight-line embusen and kiba-dachi were retained; the three-part division (Shodan to Sandan) follows Itosu's late Okinawan arrangement.
origin_person: old Shuri-te lineage (creator unknown); Anko Itosu (three-kata arrangement); Gichin Funakoshi (renaming)
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; renamed in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Kata of heaven' (or 'of the universe'): part of a projected heaven-earth-man (ten-chi-jin) series of which only 'heaven' was completed, expressing fundamentals as the root of everything above them.
name: Ten no Kata
note: A wartime training innovation in two halves: omote, performed solo, and ura, performed with a partner, making it one of the first Japanese karate kata designed explicitly around paired application. Development is generally attributed to Gigo Funakoshi under his father's name; it remains central in Shotokai and is preserved in parts of Shotokan.

meaning: Commonly glossed as 'turning/rolling the body', reflecting the kata's characteristic evasive rotation; kanji and translation are not consistently documented.
name: Tenshin
note: Chito-ryu lineage research treats Tenshin as probably Chitose's own composition, alongside his distinctive reworkings of Rohai and Sochin which differ enough from Okinawan versions to be considered his creations. It encapsulates the style's medical-anatomical rationale for lighter, rotational body mechanics.

meaning: 'King's crown': a name of Tomari-te origin sometimes linked (folklore) to Ryukyuan court patronage; Funakoshi's proposed rename Shofu ('pine wind') did not survive.
name: Wankan (Shotokan)
note: Shotokan's shortest kata, generally attributed to Gigo Funakoshi as an unfinished reworking of the Tomari Wankan; it entered the standard JKA syllabus after the war. The Shito-ryu line preserves the fuller Tomari form under Mabuni's name Matsukaze.
origin_person: Tomari-te lineage (Matsumora line); Shotokan version by Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; Shotokan version Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Akamine's nunchaku'. Composed by Akamine Eisuke (1925-1999), Taira Shinken's successor as head of the Ryukyu Kobudo Hozon Shinko Kai, as a second, more elaborate nunchaku kata for his Shinbukan curriculum.
name: Akamine no Nunchaku
note: Akamine, who inherited Taira's organisation in 1970, added several forms of his own; this kata passed into the Tesshinkan through his student Tamayose Hidemi.

meaning: 'Staff of Yara of Chatan'. Named for Chatan Yara (traditionally 1668-1756), the Chatan bushi who studied martial arts in China and is a pivotal early figure of Okinawan weapon arts; the kata preserves the bojutsu of his line.
name: Chatan Yara no Kon
note: Attributed to Chatan Yara by all major lineage histories, though the connection is traditional; the surviving form was fixed within Taira Shinken's Ryukyu Kobudo.
origin_place: Chatan, Okinawa (methods attributed to study in Fuzhou, China)

meaning: 'Sai of Yara of Chatan'. Attributed to Chatan Yara, the early 18th-century Chatan bushi trained in China; today the most famous sai kata in the world through its use in elite kata competition.
name: Chatan Yara no Sai
note: Preserved in Taira Shinken's compilation and also taught by Shimabuku Tatsuo within Isshin-ryu kobudo; the attribution to Chatan Yara himself is traditional. A karate kata of the same name (Chatan Yara Kusanku) shares the eponym.

meaning: 'Staff of Chinen of Shikiyanaka'. Named for a 19th-century bo master of the Chinen family (the family behind the Yamane-ryu bo tradition), identified by his residence at Shikiyanaka; the kata preserves his personal bojutsu.
name: Chinen Shikiyanaka no Kon
note: Preserved both within Taira Shinken's Ryukyu Kobudo and in the Yamane line, where the Chinen family transmission ran Chinen Umikana to Chinen Sanda to Chinen Masami, who named the style Yamane-ryu.
origin_person: Chinen Shikiyanaka, bo master of the Chinen family

meaning: 'Sai of Hamahiga'. Named for Hamahiga Pechin, a martial artist of Hamahiga Island (17th-18th century by tradition) credited with both a sai and a tonfa kata; the paired attribution makes him one of the earliest named kobudo figures.
name: Hamahiga no Sai
note: Tradition links Hamahiga (Hama Higa) to a demonstration before Satsuma officials, but his biography is folkloric; the surviving kata was fixed within Taira Shinken's Ryukyu Kobudo.

meaning: 'Tonfa of Hamahiga'. The classical tonfa kata attributed to Hamahiga Pechin of Hamahiga Island, the same traditional figure credited with Hamahiga no Sai; the oldest named tonfa form in Okinawan kobudo.
name: Hamahiga no Tonfa
note: Fixed in Taira Shinken's Ryukyu Kobudo and carried into Isshin-ryu (as Hamahiga no Tuifa) by Shimabuku Tatsuo; Hamahiga's biography is folkloric.

meaning: 'Sai of Hantagwa' ('the little one from the cliff edge' in Okinawan). Named for Tsuken Hantagwa (also linked with Tsuken Koragwa), a sai man of the Tsuken Island tradition.
name: Hantagwa no Sai
note: A rare kata of the Tsuken Island cluster preserved in Taira-line dojo; the identities of Hantagwa and Koragwa rest wholly on oral tradition (folklore). [Verifier: Kata confirmed in the RKHSK sai list (Hantagwa no Sai) and linked to the Tsuken tradition; the specific Okinawan etymology ('little one from the cliff edge') and Koragwa link are lore-level, unverified.]

meaning: 'Sai of Jigen'. An advanced sai kata of the Ryukyu Kobudo compilation whose eponym is obscure; sometimes explained as a personal name, sometimes given a Buddhist reading ('eye of compassion').
name: Jigen no Sai
note: Taught at senior level in the Akamine (Shinbukan) line; its pre-Taira history is undocumented and the name's origin is disputed. [Verifier: Confirmed in the RKHSK sai list; the eponym genuinely is obscure, so the hedged meaning is fair, but neither explanation could be verified.]

meaning: 'Hand (art) of the sickle' in Okinawan. The Matayoshi kama kata codifying peasant twin-sickle methods, with the rope-and-sickle (kusarigama-like) usage retained in advanced practice.
name: Kama nu Ti
note: Matayoshi Shinko gathered village kama methods during his early 20th-century travels; Shinpo fixed the numbered forms taught in the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei.

meaning: 'Kanegawa's pair of sickles'. Named for a kama expert remembered as Kanegawa (Kanigawa); nichogama means 'two sickles', the paired farming implements wielded together. The principal classical kama kata of Ryukyu Kobudo.
name: Kanegawa no Nichogama
note: The same traditional figure is credited with the tinbe kata Kanegawa no Tinbe; both reached the present through Taira Shinken's compilation and continue in the Akamine and Tesshinkan lines.

meaning: 'Kanegawa's shield'. The tinbe-rochin kata of Ryukyu Kobudo, pairing a small shield (historically turtle shell or woven cane) with the short spear rochin; named for the same traditional figure as Kanegawa no Nichogama.
name: Kanegawa no Tinbe
note: The only classical shield kata in the Taira compilation; its survival is credited to Taira's preservation work, with the eponymous Kanegawa known solely from oral tradition.

meaning: 'Sai of the Kojo family'. Named for the Kojo (Kugusuku) family of Kume village, Naha, descendants of Chinese immigrants who maintained a private family martial tradition (Kojo-ryu); the kata preserves their saijutsu.
name: Kojo no Sai
note: The Kojo family arts descend from the 36 families of Kume; the sai kata bearing their name entered Taira Shinken's compilation and is taught at senior level in the Akamine line.

meaning: 'Staff of the vajra (diamond thunderbolt)'. The Buddhist term kongo connotes indestructibility; the kata is Taira Shinken's own synthesis, composed as a summative advanced bo form for his Ryukyu Kobudo.
name: Kongo no Kon
note: One of the few kata Taira openly composed himself rather than compiled; transmitted through Akamine Eisuke's Shinbukan and the Tesshinkan as a senior grading kata.

meaning: 'Kusanku with sai'. Shimabuku Tatsuo's transposition of the empty-hand kata Kusanku (named for the 18th-century Chinese envoy Kong Xiangjun) onto the sai, retaining its night-fighting associations while exploiting the sai's trapping and flipping actions.
name: Kusanku Sai
note: A modern creation unique to Isshin-ryu kobudo, built on the Kusanku kata Shimabuku learned from Kyan Chotoku and the saijutsu he learned from Taira Shinken and Kina Shosei.

meaning: 'Hand (art) of the hoe'. The Matayoshi kata for the farmer's hoe (kuwa), turning digging, dragging and handle-butt actions into fighting technique; a showpiece of the peasant-implement side of Okinawan kobudo.
name: Kuwa nu Ti
note: Almost unique to the Matayoshi line; Shinko is said to have codified village hoe methods, and Shinpo standardised the kata taught today.

era: first half of the 20th century; fixed c. 1956
meaning: 'Kyan's sai'. Isshin-ryu sai kata named in honour of Kyan Chotoku, Shimabuku Tatsuo's principal karate teacher; it encodes the sai basics Shimabuku attributed to Kyan's circle.
name: Kyan no Sai
note: The attribution is debated: some Isshin-ryu historians trace the material to Kina Shosei's Ufuchiku line rather than to Kyan himself. Treated here as an Isshin-ryu codification with a traditional eponym.
origin_person: attributed to the circle of Kyan Chotoku; assembled by Shimabuku Tatsuo

meaning: 'Maezato's nunchaku'. Maezato was Taira Shinken's birth surname (he took his mother's name Taira later), so the kata is self-named: his own codification of the horse-bridle flail into a formal kata.
name: Maezato no Nunchaku
note: Little classical nunchaku kata survived into the 20th century; Taira composed this form (and Maezato no Tekko) under his birth name to fill the gap in his 1955 Ryukyu Kobudo syllabus.

meaning: 'Maezato's knuckle-dusters'. Tekko are stirrup- or horseshoe-derived fist-load weapons; Taira Shinken composed this, the only widely practised tekko kata, under his birth name Maezato.
name: Maezato no Tekko
note: Composed by Taira to give the tekko a formal kata within his 42-kata Ryukyu Kobudo compilation; performed today in the Akamine and Tesshinkan lines and adopted by many karate schools.

meaning: 'Swastika sai', from the manji (卍) silhouette formed when the sai are held in reverse grip with arms extended in opposite directions. Composed by Taira Shinken as an advanced synthesis of his sai material.
name: Manji no Sai
note: Along with Kongo no Kon, one of Taira's acknowledged own compositions; a capstone sai kata in the Akamine and Tesshinkan syllabi.

meaning: 'Matayoshi nunchaku'. The Matayoshi line's flail kata, shorter and more utilitarian than the Taira-line forms, reflecting the weapon's origin as a horse bridle or threshing tool.
name: Matayoshi no Nunchaku
note: Codified within the family curriculum and fixed by Matayoshi Shinpo after 1960 for the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei. [Verifier: The Matayoshi line does have its own nunchaku kata, shorter than Taira-line forms, and the bridle/threshing origin is standard lore; details of Shinko's authorship are traditional rather than documented.]

meaning: 'Matayoshi sai'. The graded sai kata of the Matayoshi curriculum (dai ichi and dai ni, plus the three-sai form Sancho Sai in which a third sai is carried for throwing), blending Okinawan saijutsu with Chinese methods from the Kingai-ryu inheritance.
name: Matayoshi no Sai
note: Matayoshi Shinko assembled the family sai material from Okinawan teachers (including the Agena/Gushikawa tradition) and his studies in China; his son Shinpo fixed the numbered kata taught today through the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei. [Verifier: Matayoshi sai kata exist (commonly listed as Nicho Sai and Sancho Sai, the latter with a third throwing sai); the 'dai ichi/dai ni' naming is branch-depende
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa (with Chinese elements from Fuzhou)

meaning: 'Matayoshi tonfa' (tunkua is the Okinawan name of the millstone-handle weapon). The paired kata dai ichi and dai ni codify the Matayoshi family's tonfa method, marked by circular flywheel strikes and simultaneous double-arm actions.
name: Matayoshi no Tunkua
note: Assembled by Matayoshi Shinko from rural Okinawan tonfa methods and fixed as two numbered kata by Matayoshi Shinpo for the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei curriculum.

meaning: 'Nunti' (a six-foot staff mounted with a manji-shaped sai head, derived from a fishing gaff). The kata codifies thrusting, hooking and trapping methods unique to this fisherman's weapon, with paired manji sai often thrown or held in the belt.
name: Nunti
note: The nunti is emblematic of the Matayoshi school's preservation of fishing- and farming-implement arts; Shinko gathered the methods during his travels and Shinpo fixed the kata for the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei.

meaning: 'Sakugawa's staff'. Named for Sakugawa Kanga ('Tode' Sakugawa), the Shuri bushi who studied in Qing China and stands at the head of the Shuri-te lineage; the kata preserves the bojutsu credited to him and is a cornerstone of every major kobudo line.
name: Sakugawa no Kon
note: Taira's Ryukyu Kobudo transmits sho/chu/dai versions; the Yamane-ryu line transmits its own fluid version through Chinen Sanda and Chinen Masami. Direct authorship by Sakugawa is traditional rather than documented.
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa (methods attributed to study in Qing China)

meaning: 'Three-section staff, number one'. Kata for the Chinese sanjiegun, three staves linked by cord or chain; its presence in Okinawan kobudo comes from Matayoshi Shinko's training in Fuzhou under the monk Kingai.
name: Sansetsukon Dai Ichi
note: Part of the Kingai-ryu inheritance (with tinbe, suruchin and nunti) that distinguishes Matayoshi kobudo from the Taira compilation; accounts of Shinko's Chinese travels blend documented fact with family tradition. [Verifier: The Matayoshi line does practise a sansetsukon kata from Shinko's Kingai-ryu training in Fuzhou, which matches; the 'Dai Ichi' numbering and the precise 1911-1934 China dates
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China; codified in Naha, Okinawa

meaning: 'Staff of Sesoko'. Named for Sesoko Island (Motobu) or a bo man from it; a rare, advanced kata of the Taira compilation.
name: Sesoko no Kon
note: One of the rarer bo kata preserved by Taira Shinken and carried on in the Akamine line; its pre-Taira transmission is undocumented.

meaning: 'Shirotaru's staff'. Named for Shirotaru (Shirataru), a bo expert of the old Ryukyu kingdom whose biography is lost; some traditions place him in Tomari or as a student in the Sakugawa line.
name: Shirotaru no Kon
note: Exists in sho and dai versions in Taira Shinken's Ryukyu Kobudo and in distinct Yamane-ryu versions transmitted through Chinen Sanda and Chinen Masami. The attribution to a person named Shirotaru is traditional. [Verifier: Real kata (Shirotaru sho/dai in Taira line, Shirataru in Yamanni-ryu, supporting the Chinen Sanda 'brought' role); the Tomari/Sakugawa-line biography is speculative lore, correc

meaning: 'Shoun's staff' (read Choun in the Matayoshi line). Named for a master remembered only as Shoun/Choun, by some accounts a Chinese sailor or settler; an old-style (koryu) kata with distinctive circular strikes.
name: Shoun no Kon
note: The Matayoshi line transmits Choun no Kun as a senior bo kata; a cognate Shoun no Kon survives in Ryukyu Kobudo lines and a version is also claimed in the Yamane tradition. The eponym is known only from oral tradition (folklore). [Verifier: Real kata (Choun no Kon in Matayoshi and Taira lines, Shoun in the Inoue line). But Motobu Naoki attributes it to Choun Uekata, a Tomari samurai c. 250 years a
origin_person: Shoun (Choun), identity uncertain, possibly a Chinese settler

meaning: 'Shushi's staff, major': the longer, more advanced of the paired versions attributed to the Chinese master Shushi (Zhou). One of the most widely practised bo kata in Okinawa and a standard competition form.
name: Shushi no Kon Dai
note: The Matayoshi line (Shushi no Kun) and the Yamane line (Suuji nu Kun, via Chinen Sanda) each transmit a single independent version that predates Taira's sho/dai split; the three versions differ markedly in rhythm and technique.
origin_person: Shushi (Zhou), a Chinese settler in Okinawa (traditional attribution)

meaning: 'Shushi's staff, minor'. Named for Shushi (Zhou, 周), traditionally a Chinese master resident in Okinawa; 'kon' is the Okinawan reading for the six-foot staff. Sho denotes the shorter of the paired versions fixed by Taira Shinken, usually the first bo kata taught in Ryukyu Kobudo.
name: Shushi no Kon Sho
note: Transmitted through Yabiku Moden's Ryukyu Kobujutsu Kenkyukai to Taira Shinken, who codified the sho/dai pair within his 1955 syllabus. The identity of Shushi rests on oral tradition only (folklore).
origin_person: Shushi (Zhou), a Chinese settler in Okinawa (traditional attribution)

meaning: 'Soeishi's staff'. Named for Soeishi Ryotoku, an 18th-century Shuri official said to have served the Ryukyuan king as secretary and bojutsu instructor; the kata is regarded as a court (samurai-class) staff tradition rather than a village one.
name: Soeishi no Kon
note: Preserved in sho and dai versions in Taira Shinken's syllabus. Isshin-ryu's bo kata Shishi no Kun is generally held to derive from Soeishi no Kon, which Shimabuku Tatsuo learned from Taira in the late 1950s.

meaning: 'Sueyoshi's staff'. Named for a bo expert associated with Sueyoshi in Shuri; an advanced Ryukyu Kobudo kata characterised by unusual grips and thrusting work.
name: Sueyoshi no Kon
note: Preserved through Taira Shinken's compilation and taught mainly at senior level in the Akamine (Shinbukan) and Tesshinkan lines; nothing verifiable is recorded of the eponymous Sueyoshi.

meaning: 'Sand-flinging staff'. A bo rendering of the sand-kicking (sunakake) tactic of the oar tradition of Tsuken Island, in which sand is flicked at an opponent's eyes before striking.
name: Sunakake no Kon
note: Practised in some Ryukyu Kobudo lines as a bo counterpart of Tsuken Sunakake no Eku; its independent history apart from the oar kata is thin and largely a 20th-century codification. [Verifier: A bo kata of this name was listed by Taira in his 1938 Karate-do Taikan chapter (three versions existed), but it was not in the standardised RKHSK syllabus, so 'Taira standardised' overstates; the eku-tactic

meaning: 'Tawada's sai'. Named for Tawada Shinboku (also given as Shinbuku, c. 1814-1884), a Shuri bushi and student of Matsumura Sokon renowned for his sai; the kata preserves his personal saijutsu.
name: Tawada no Sai
note: Lineage histories place Tawada in the circle of Matsumura Sokon; his sai method reached Taira Shinken's compilation via the early 20th-century preservation movement and remains a senior kata in the Akamine line. [Verifier: Real Taira-line kata attributed to Tawada Pechin (Shinboku), a Matsumura student famed for sai; his exact dates (c. 1814-1884) vary across sources and could not be independently

meaning: 'Shield (and short spear)'. The Matayoshi line's tinbe-rochin kata, using a turtle-shell shield and short hooked spear; its low, evasive circling is attributed to the Chinese methods Matayoshi Shinko absorbed in Fuzhou.
name: Tinbe (Matayoshi)
note: Part of the material linked to Shinko's studies with the monk Kingai in Fuzhou (the Kingai-ryu inheritance); fixed for public teaching by Shinpo Matayoshi.
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa; Chinese elements from Fuzhou

meaning: 'Tokumine's staff'. Named for Tokumine Pechin, a Shuri bushi and celebrated bo fighter exiled to Yaeyama in the late 19th century after a brawl; the kata is the signature bo form of Isshin-ryu.
name: Tokumine no Kun
note: Kyan Chotoku travelled to Yaeyama to learn Tokumine's bo; by the common story Tokumine had died and Kyan learned the kata from Tokumine's landlord (folklore). Kyan taught it to Shimabuku Tatsuo, who fixed it in Isshin-ryu.
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; transmitted from Yaeyama exile

meaning: 'Sai of Shitahaku of Tsuken'. Named for Shitahaku, a sai expert associated with Tsuken Island (or a Shuri official of the Shitahaku family); usually the first classical sai kata of Ryukyu Kobudo.
name: Tsuken Shitahaku no Sai
note: Transmitted through Yabiku Moden to Taira Shinken, who placed it at the base of the Ryukyu Kobudo sai curriculum; the historical Shitahaku is known only from lineage tradition.

meaning: 'Sand-flinging oar of Tsuken'. The classical kata for the eku (fisherman's oar), whose signature technique scoops sand into an attacker's eyes; named for Tsuken Akachu ('the red-faced man of Tsuken'), a legendary oarsman-fighter of Tsuken Island.
name: Tsuken Sunakake no Eku
note: Folklore casts Akachu as a fisherman who defeated an armed bushi with his oar. The Taira line fixed Tsuken Sunakake no Eku; the Matayoshi line transmits its own version as Chikin Akachu no Eku Dii, both claiming the same origin.
origin_person: Tsuken Akachu, oarsman of Tsuken Island (legendary)

meaning: 'Staff of Tsuken'. Named for Tsuken Island off the Katsuren peninsula and its famed bo tradition, personified by Tsuken Seisoku (Shosoku) Oyakata, an 18th-century official; a direct, combative kata regarded as one of the oldest bo forms.
name: Tsuken no Kon
note: Village bo traditions of Tsuken Island produced several named forms (including versions linked to Tsuken Hantagwa and Tsuken Koragwa); Taira Shinken and the Matayoshi line each fixed their own Tsuken bo kata. Attribution to a single creator is folkloric.
origin_person: Tsuken Seisoku (Shosoku) Oyakata of Tsuken Island

meaning: 'Sai of the Ufuchiku' (Ufuchiku was the title of the chief of palace police at Shuri). Preserves the saijutsu of Kanagusuku Sanda (1841-1926), the last Ufuchiku, whose duties made the sai a true policing weapon rather than a demonstration piece.
name: Ufuchiku no Sai
note: Kanagusuku, by tradition a bodyguard of King Sho Tai (folklore embellishes this role), passed his art to Kina Shosei (1882-1981), who preserved it as Ufuchiku Kobujutsu; Isa Kaishu and Kyan Shinyei continued the line. [Verifier: Ufuchiku Kobudo (sai-centred) founded by Kanagusuku/Kinjo Sanda, transmitted via Kina Shosei then Isa Kaishu, is confirmed; a kata under this exact name is attested only i

meaning: 'Staff of Urasoe' (Urashi is the Okinawan pronunciation of Urasoe). Associated by tradition with Uhugushiku (Ufugusuku, 'great castle'), a bushi connected with Urasoe castle; a vigorous kata noted for its jumping strike.
name: Urashi no Kon
note: Taira Shinken fixed the Ryukyu Kobudo version, which Shimabuku Tatsuo carried into Isshin-ryu as Urashi Bo; the Matsumura Seito line of Soken Hohan preserves a related Ufugushiku no Kun. The link between the Urashi and Ufugushiku traditions is asserted by lineage histories rather than documents. [Verifier: Kata is real (Urasoe no Kon in Taira line, Urashi Bo in Isshin-ryu) with its noted jump; the
origin_person: Uhugushiku (Ufugusuku), bushi associated with Urasoe (traditional attribution)

meaning: 'Sai of Yaka'. Named for a sai expert from Yaka (Kin district) remembered only by his place name; a compact kata of the Taira compilation.
name: Yaka no Sai
note: Preserved through Taira Shinken and prominent in the Akamine (Shinbukan) and Tesshinkan grading syllabi; nothing verifiable is recorded of the eponym.

meaning: 'Tonfa of Yara the younger' (the diminutive -guwa distinguishes him from the elder Chatan Yara). Tradition links the kata to a descendant or junior namesake of Chatan Yara; a fast, close-quarters tonfa form.
name: Yaraguwa no Tonfa
note: Whether Yaraguwa was Chatan Yara himself in youth, a grandson, or an unrelated namesake is unresolved in the lineage literature; the form survives through Taira Shinken's compilation. [Verifier: Real Taira-line kata (Yaragwa no Tonfa). But the entry is internally inconsistent: the meaning says a junior namesake of Chatan Yara while introduced_by credits Chatan Yara himself as creator; sources spli
origin_person: Yaraguwa ('young Yara'), traditionally of the Chatan Yara line

meaning: 'Yonegawa's staff' (Yunigawa in Okinawan). Named for a bo expert remembered only as Yonegawa; a long, technically demanding kata noted for its one-handed techniques and level changes.
name: Yonegawa no Kon
note: Transmitted to Taira Shinken through Yabiku Moden; the Yamane line preserves its own Yunigawa version through the Chinen family. Nothing reliable is recorded of the eponymous Yonegawa.

era: Passai 18th-19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'To extract from (or storm) a fortress': the name evokes breaking through an enemy stronghold, reflected in the kata's driving, penetrating techniques.
name: Bassai
note: The Korean form follows Itosu's Passai Dai as transmitted in Shotokan (Bassai Dai); it is the signature mid-dan hyung of Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do and appears as Pal Che or Palsek in kwan-era taekwondo syllabi. Attribution of the original Passai is contested Okinawan tradition rather than documented fact.
origin_person: Attributed variously to Sokon Matsumura and Oyadomari lineages (origin uncertain)
origin_place: Shuri/Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Seven stars', referring to the Big Dipper (seven-star constellation), symbolising guidance and the connection of the practitioner to the cosmos; seven forms blending hard karate-derived technique with soft, breath-led Chinese-style movement.
name: Chil Sung series
note: Hwang Kee's own creation, drawing on his study of northern Chinese arts and Yang-style-influenced soft movement, designed to express his philosophy of Neh Gung (internal) and Weh Gung (external) energy; they became the signature hyung of Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan.
variants: Chil Sung Il Ro to Chil Ro

meaning: Named for General Choi Yong, premier and commander-in-chief of the Goryeo armed forces, revered for loyalty and patriotism and executed by subordinates led by Yi Song-gye, later first king of Joseon. 46 movements.
name: Choi-Yong
note: Third-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring the incorruptible Goryeo general.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Heaven and Earth': in Asian cosmology the creation of the world and the beginning of human history; as the beginner's first pattern its two similar halves represent heaven and earth. 19 movements.
name: Chon-Ji
note: First of the 24 Chang Hon tul, developed by Choi Hong-hi with military pioneers of the Oh Do Kwan (Nam Tae-hi foremost) to replace the Japanese kata inherited by the kwans.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Heaven's fist' or sky: heaven as the origin of all creation and the object of ancient Korean reverence; the movements evoke an eagle soaring and pious gestures towards the sky.
name: Chonkwon
note: Seventh-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

meaning: Pseudonym of General Kim Duk-ryang of the Yi (Joseon) dynasty; the pattern ends with a left-hand attack to symbolise the tragedy of his death at 27 in prison before reaching maturity. 52 movements.
name: Choong-Jang
note: Second-dan pattern; the ITF Encyclopedia dates Kim Duk-ryang to the 14th century though historically he lived 1567-1596.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: The posthumous title of Admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545-1598), inventor of the armoured turtle ship (1592); the pattern ends with a left-hand attack to symbolise his regrettable death before he could show his full potential. 30 movements.
name: Choong-Moo
note: Among the earliest Chang Hon patterns; the last coloured-belt tul in the ITF syllabus.

era: Naihanchi 19th century or earlier; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Iron horse(man)': a Korean coinage echoing the Japanese Tekki (iron knight), describing the kata's rooted horse-riding stance performed along a single lateral line.
name: Chul Ki series
note: Derives from Naihanchi, the old core kata of Shuri-te associated with Sokon Matsumura and split into three by Itosu; the kwans received it as Shotokan's Tekki and renamed it Chul Ki. Still practised at dan level in Tang Soo Do and Soo Bahk Do.
origin_person: Unknown Okinawan/Chinese origin; standardised by Anko Itosu
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
variants: Chulgi Cho Dan / E Dan / Sam Dan

meaning: 'Short fist', 'long fist' and 'eight-technique fist': Korean forms of Chinese quanfa (kwon bup) sets, preserving the changquan/chuan-fa material Yoon Byung-in learned in Manchuria alongside his Shudokan karate.
name: Dan Kwon / Jang Kwon / Palgi Kwon
native: 단권 (短拳) / 장권 (長拳) / 팔기권 (八技拳)
note: Yoon Byung-in, who studied chuan-fa in Manchuria and karate under Toyama Kanken's Shudokan, taught these quanfa-derived forms in the YMCA Kwon Bup Bu/Chang Moo Kwan; after his disappearance in the Korean War his students Park Chul-hee and Hong Jong-pyo preserved them in the Kang Duk Won. They mark the only substantial non-karate Chinese stream in the kwan-era curriculum. [Verifier: The forms are r

meaning: Named for Dangun, the legendary founder of Korea in 2333 BC; unusually, all its punches are high section, said to symbolise Dangun scaling a mountain. 21 movements.
name: Dan-Gun
note: Second Chang Hon pattern; the Dangun founding legend it honours is national mythology, cited as such in the ITF Encyclopedia.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Pseudonym of the patriot Ahn Chang-ho (1876-1938), who devoted his life to education and the Korean independence movement; the 24 movements represent his entire life.
name: Do-San
note: Early Chang Hon pattern honouring the independence educator Ahn Chang-ho (Dosan).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Pseudonym of Son Byong-hi, leader of the 1 March 1919 independence movement; the 45 movements refer to his age when he renamed Donghak as Chondogyo in 1905, and the diagram represents indomitable spirit.
name: Eui-Am
note: Second-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring the religious and independence leader Son Byong-hi (Uiam).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Named for Gyebaek, the great general of Baekje (died 660 AD); the diagram represents his severe and strict military discipline. 44 movements.
name: Ge-Baek
note: First-dan pattern honouring the Baekje general who fought to the death at Hwangsanbeol.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Water' (also evoking the Han river and 'han' as Korea itself): adaptability, continuity and the strength of water that nurtures life yet wears down stone.
name: Hansu
note: Eighth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

meaning: Commonly glossed as 'flower goodness' or 'harmonious virtue'; the most advanced Soo Bahk Do hyung, expressing the Kwon Bup (fist method) chapter of the Muye Dobo Tongji in flowing, mature movement.
name: Hwa Sun
note: Hwang Kee's master-level creation derived from his interpretation of the Kwon Bup illustrations in the Muye Dobo Tongji; reserved for senior dan grades in the World Moo Duk Kwan. The name's translation varies across the organisation's own literature. [Verifier: Hwa Sun exists as the most advanced Soo Bahk Do hyung, created by Hwang Kee from the Kwon Bup section of the Muye Dobo Tongji (verified).

meaning: Named for the Hwarang, the youth warrior corps of Silla (7th century) whose code inspired Korean martial ethics; the 29 movements refer to the 29th Infantry Division, where taekwondo developed into maturity.
name: Hwa-Rang
note: One of the very first Chang Hon patterns, worked out in the army's 29th Division by Choi Hong-hi and Nam Tae-hi; its military birthplace is encoded in the movement count.

meaning: 'Oneness': the thought of the Silla monk Wonhyo that body and mind, spirit and substance are one; the highest state of taekwondo, with a floor pattern based on the Buddhist swastika (卍).
name: Ilyeo
note: Ninth-dan and final Kukkiwon poomsae, framing mastery as spiritual unification; honours the same monk as the ITF pattern Won-Hyo.

meaning: 'Mercy and grace' (慈恩): traditionally linked to the Jion-ji Buddhist temple, suggesting monastic transmission of the Jion kata group (Jion, Jiin, Jitte).
name: Ji On
note: Received in Korea through Shotokan's Jion; a dan-level hyung in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do. The temple origin is tradition rather than documented history.
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

era: Chintō mid-19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: Korean reading of Chintō, traditionally the name of a shipwrecked Chinese sailor whose fighting method Sokon Matsumura codified; Funakoshi's rename Gankaku ('crane on a rock') describes its one-legged crane stances.
name: Jin Do
note: The Tang Soo Do version follows the Itosu/Shito-ryu-line Chinto pattern more than Shotokan's Gankaku, reflecting the mixed Japanese sources of the kwans; the Chintō shipwreck story is Okinawan folklore. A senior dan hyung in Moo Duk Kwan.
origin_person: Attributed to Sokon Matsumura, from the sailor Chintō (folklore)
origin_place: Tomari/Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Earth' (literally 'treading the earth'): all life springs from and returns to the earth; the poomsae depicts a man standing on the ground reaching towards the sky.
name: Jitae
note: Sixth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

meaning: Named for the patriot Ahn Jung-geun, who assassinated Resident-General Ito Hirobumi in 1909; the 32 movements represent his age when he was executed at Lushun prison in 1910.
name: Joong-Gun
note: Sixth Chang Hon pattern, honouring the independence martyr Ahn Jung-geun.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: The philosophical idea that man is master of everything and decides everything, which Choi linked to Baekdu Mountain, symbol of the Korean spirit; the diagram represents the mountain. 45 movements.
name: Juche
note: Replaced Ko-Dang in the 24-pattern set in the mid-1980s after Choi's rapprochement with North Korea; because Juche is the DPRK state ideology, several ITF branches and Chang Hon offshoots retain Ko-Dang instead or practise both.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the ITF technical committee

meaning: 'Diamond' (vajra): hardness that cannot be broken and brightness, also evoking Mt Keumgang; the floor pattern is the Chinese character for mountain (山) and its slow keumgang blocks express immovable spirit.
name: Keumgang
note: Second-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

meaning: 'Foundation forms'. Three elementary I-pattern forms teaching low block, middle punch and stance turning; the Korean counterpart of the Shotokan Taikyoku series.
name: Kicho Hyung
note: Modelled on the Taikyoku kata of Shotokan, which the kwan founders learned in Japan or from Funakoshi's books; Hwang Kee formalised them as Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu, E Bu and Sam Bu in the Moo Duk Kwan. Most kwans used equivalents as first-geup forms before the Pyung Ahn series.
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi and Gigo Funakoshi (Taikyoku model); adapted by Hwang Kee and Won Kuk Lee
origin_place: Tokyo, Japan; adapted in Seoul, Korea
variants: Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu / E Bu / Sam Bu

era: By 1972; removed from the official 24 c. 1986
meaning: Pseudonym of the patriot Cho Man-sik (1883-1950), who dedicated his life to the independence movement and education; the 39 movements refer to his imprisonments and his birthplace on the 39th degree of latitude.
name: Ko-Dang
note: Original member of the Chang Hon set replaced by Juche in the mid-1980s; ironically Cho Man-sik was executed in North Korea, and many non-ITF Chang Hon organisations (and post-2002 ITF branches) still teach Ko-Dang.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

era: Kata c. 1760s-1800s; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: The Korean reading of the Chinese characters 公相君 (Kusanku), the honorific title of a Chinese envoy to Okinawa c. 1756 whose fighting method inspired the kata; the Koreans preserved the older personal name rather than Funakoshi's rename Kanku ('viewing the sky').
name: Kong Sang Koon
note: Transmitted to Korea as Shotokan's Kanku Dai but retained under its Okinawan name in Korean reading; it is the longest and most senior of the classical Tang Soo Do hyung. The story of the envoy Kusanku teaching his art is early tradition recorded in the Oshima Hikki (1762).
origin_person: Kata attributed to Tode Sakugawa, after the envoy Kusanku
origin_place: Okinawa (Chinese influence via Fuzhou); brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: Named for the Goryeo dynasty (918-1392), which repelled the Mongol invasions and gave Korea its name; symbolises the conviction of the seonbae (learned man). Its floor pattern is the Chinese character for 'scholar' (士).
name: Koryo
note: First-dan Kukkiwon poomsae; the 1967 'Original Koryo' created with the Palgwae set was replaced by the present Koryo when the Taegeuk system was adopted, and the older form survives only as a historical curiosity.

meaning: Named for Gwanggaeto the Great, 19th king of Goguryeo, who recovered lost territories including much of Manchuria; the 39 movements refer to the first two figures of 391 AD, the year he came to the throne.
name: Kwang-Gae
note: First-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring the expansionist Goguryeo king.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Honours King Munmu, 30th king of Silla, whose body was buried near the Great King's Rock so his soul would become a sea dragon defending Korea; the 61 movements refer to the last two figures of 661 AD, when he came to the throne.
name: Moon-Moo
note: Fourth-dan pattern noted for its extremely slow, controlled kicks; the underwater-tomb story is Silla legend attached to a real site (Daewangam).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': direct Korean reading of Gojushiho (五十四歩), the number 54 having Buddhist significance (half of 108); the kata's flowing, drunken-crane movements are among the most advanced in the Shuri-te canon.
name: O Sip Sa Bo
note: The highest classical karate-derived hyung in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do/Soo Bahk Do, deriving from Useishi/Gojushiho of the Matsumura-Itosu line as transmitted in Japanese karate.
origin_person: Shuri-te transmission via Sokon Matsumura and Anko Itosu
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Eight trigrams' (palgwae = bagua): eight forms keyed to the eight trigrams of the I Ching, from Keon (heaven) to Gon (earth), representing the full range of natural phenomena.
name: Palgwae series
note: The KTA's first unified coloured-belt set, drafted by a committee drawn from a subset of kwans (including Lee Chong-woo of Jidokwan and Lee Kyo-yoon of Hanmookwan, with Kwak Kun-sik, Hyun Jong-myun, Park Hae-man, Kim Soon-bae and others); because major kwans were unrepresented, an expanded committee replaced the set with the Taegeuk poomsae in 1971-1972, though many schools still teach Palgwae.
variants: Palgwae Il Jang to Pal Jang

meaning: Pseudonym of the loyal subject and poet Jeong Mong-ju (1337-1392), famed for the line 'I would not serve a second master though I might be crucified a hundred times'; the diagram represents his unerring loyalty. 36 movements.
name: Po-Eun
note: First-dan pattern performed entirely on one line, honouring the Goryeo loyalist Jeong Mong-ju (Poeun).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Vast plain': the open, fertile plain that sustains life, expressing majesty and abundance; performed on a single line.
name: Pyongwon
note: Fourth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

era: Created c. 1904-1907; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence' or 'safety and calm': the Korean reading of Pinan (平安), Itosu's name expressing that mastery of the five forms lets one defend oneself with a calm mind.
name: Pyung Ahn series
note: Itosu's five Pinan (drawn largely from Kusanku and Channan) reached Korea as Shotokan's Heian through Won Kuk Lee (Chung Do Kwan) and Byung Jick Ro (Song Moo Kwan), both Funakoshi students, while Hwang Kee learned them substantially from Japanese karate books; Yun Kwae-byung's Ji Do Kwan transmitted Shudokan/Shito-ryu versions. They remain the core geup forms of Tang Soo Do and early taekwondo.
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
variants: Pyung Ahn Cho Dan to Oh Dan

meaning: 'Sign (vision) of the white heron': the one-legged stances mimic a heron standing in water; Funakoshi renamed his version Meikyo ('bright mirror').
name: Ro Hai
note: Korean versions derive from the Itosu Rohai line carried through Shito-ryu/Shudokan teachers of the kwan founders (notably Yun Kwae-byung of the Ji Do Kwan) and through Hwang Kee's study; practised at dan level in Tang Soo Do.
origin_person: Tomari-te kata associated with Kosaku Matsumora; three versions standardised by Anko Itosu
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Four-direction punch' and 'four-direction block': pre-pattern fundamental exercises teaching turning, blocking and punching to the four compass points before the student learns Chon-Ji.
name: Saju Jirugi / Saju Makgi
note: Introductory exercises of the Chang Hon system, codified in Choi Hong-hi's Taekwon-Do texts and the 1983 Encyclopedia; not counted among the 24 tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and early Oh Do Kwan instructors

meaning: Denotes the 1 March 1919 (Samil) independence movement; the 33 movements stand for the 33 patriots who planned it.
name: Sam-Il
note: Third-dan Chang Hon pattern commemorating the Samil uprising against Japanese rule.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Honours King Sejong the Great, who invented the Korean alphabet in 1443; the 24 movements refer to the 24 letters of hangul and the diagram represents 'king'.
name: Se-Jong
note: Fifth-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring Korea's greatest monarch and his alphabet.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

era: Jitte 19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Ten hands': the Korean reading of Jitte (十手), traditionally meaning one who masters the kata fights with the strength of ten men.
name: Sip Soo
note: Derives from the Tomari-te kata Jitte as codified in Shotokan; in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do it is a dan-grade hyung noted for its slow, heavy pressing techniques and bo-defence interpretations.
origin_person: Unknown; Tomari-te kata standardised through Itosu
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Decimal' or 'ten symbols': refers to the ten traditional symbols of longevity (sun, moon, mountain, water, stone, pine, herb of eternal youth, tortoise, deer and crane), signifying endless development and growth; the floor pattern is the character 十.
name: Sipjin
note: Fifth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set.

meaning: Pseudonym of the great monk Choi Hyong-ung (Seosan Daesa, 1520-1604); the 72 movements refer to his age when he organised a corps of monk soldiers with his pupil Samyeongdang to repel the Japanese invasion of 1592.
name: So-San
note: The longest Chang Hon pattern (72 movements), a fifth-dan tul honouring the warrior monk Seosan.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Pine tree and rock': evergreen strength and unbreakable stability, the pen name concept of ATA founder Haeng Ung Lee; a proprietary set of coloured-belt forms (Songahm 1-5, In Wha 1-2, Choong Jung 1-2) and black-belt forms (Shim Jun onwards) designed so each rank's form uses only that rank's techniques.
name: Songahm series
note: The American Taekwondo Association replaced its earlier Chang Hon patterns with Haeng Ung Lee's Songahm system from 1983, one of the largest bespoke forms curricula outside the ITF and Kukkiwon canons; practised only within ATA/Songahm-affiliated bodies.

meaning: 'Great brightness': the sacred mountain (identified with Mt Baekdu) where Dangun is said to have founded the Korean nation; the floor pattern (工) represents the bridge between heaven and earth.
name: Taebaek
note: Third-dan Kukkiwon poomsae; its founding-myth reference parallels the ITF pattern Dan-Gun.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Gan (☶, mountain): stability and firmness, knowing when to move and when to stop.
name: Taegeuk Chil Jang
note: Seventh Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Tae (☱, lake): inner firmness beneath outer softness and joyfulness.
name: Taegeuk Ee Jang
note: Second of the eight Taegeuk geup poomsae created by the 1971 KTA committee.

meaning: First Taegeuk poomsae, keyed to the trigram Keon (☰, heaven and yang): the beginning of all creation, hence the simplest form for the beginner.
name: Taegeuk Il Jang
note: The Taegeuk set was created by the expanded KTA poomsae committee representing all major kwans (members documented include Kwak Kun-sik, Lee Chong-woo, Lee Kyo-yoon, Park Hae-man, Hyun Jong-myun, Kim Soon-bae, Lee Yong-sup, Han Young-tae and Bae Young-ki) and became the Kukkiwon/WT geup curriculum.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Seon (☴, wind): gentle yet at times forceful, alternating soft flowing movement with sudden power.
name: Taegeuk Oh Jang
note: Fifth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Gon (☷, earth): the receptive root and end of the cycle; the final geup form consolidating all basics before black belt.
name: Taegeuk Pal Jang
note: Eighth and last Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set, completing the eight-trigram cycle begun with Keon.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Jin (☳, thunder): great power and dignity, teaching calm and courage in the face of danger.
name: Taegeuk Sa Jang
note: Fourth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Ri (☲, fire): passion, energy and brightness, expressed in faster combinations.
name: Taegeuk Sam Jang
note: Third Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set.

meaning: Keyed to the trigram Gam (☵, water): constant flow and adaptability, overcoming difficulty by yielding like water.
name: Taegeuk Yuk Jang
note: Sixth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set.

meaning: Pen name of the scholar Yi Hwang (1501-1570), authority on neo-Confucianism; the 37 movements refer to his birthplace on the 37th degree of latitude and the diagram represents 'scholar'.
name: Toi-Gye
note: Seventh Chang Hon pattern, honouring the philosopher Yi Hwang (Toegye).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: 'Unification': denotes the resolve to reunify Korea, divided since 1945; the diagram symbolises the homogeneous race. 56 movements.
name: Tong-Il
note: The final (sixth-dan) pattern of the Chang Hon system, closing the 24-tul cycle that Choi likened to the 24 hours of a day, one lifetime.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Pen name of Syngman Rhee, first president of South Korea, whom the pattern originally honoured.
name: U-Nam
note: A rare, discontinued tul appearing in Choi Hong-hi's 1959 Korean-language book; it was quietly removed after Rhee's fall from power in 1960 and never entered the 24-pattern canon, surviving only through historical reconstruction.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Named for General Eulji Mundeok, who defended Korea against a Sui invasion of nearly one million men in 612 AD using hit-and-run guerrilla tactics; the diagram represents his surname and the 42 movements Choi's age when he designed the pattern.
name: Ul-Ji
note: Fourth-dan pattern honouring the victor of the Salsu River battle.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Named for the monk Wonhyo (617-686), who introduced Buddhism to the Silla dynasty. 28 movements.
name: Won-Hyo
note: Fourth Chang Hon pattern; Wonhyo's oneness-of-mind philosophy also underlies the WT poomsae Ilyeo, a rare shared reference across the two systems.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Named for General Yeon Gaesomun of Goguryeo; the 49 movements refer to the last two figures of 649 AD, when he forced the Tang dynasty out of Korea after destroying nearly 300,000 troops at Ansi Sung.
name: Yon-Gae
note: Fourth-dan pattern honouring the Goguryeo military dictator who repelled Tang invasions.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

meaning: Named for General Kim Yu-sin of Silla; the 68 movements refer to the last two figures of 668 AD, the year of Korea's unification, and the sword-drawing ready posture on the right side symbolises his mistake of following royal orders to fight fellow Koreans with foreign (Tang) forces.
name: Yoo-Sin
note: Third-dan pattern honouring the unifier-general of Silla, with an unusually critical symbolism built into its start.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

era: Created from 1958, after Hwang Kee's 1957 discovery of the Muye Dobo Tongji
meaning: 'Six paths' or 'six-road' forms: six hyung (Du Mun, Jung Jul, Po Wol, Yang Pyun, Sal Chu, Choong Ro), each named for its governing concept, reconstructing indigenous-Korean-flavoured movement from classical texts.
name: Yuk Ro series
note: Created by Hwang Kee following his study of the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790 Korean military manual) found in the Seoul National University library in 1957; intended to root Soo Bahk Do in Korean rather than Japanese sources. The forms are modern creations inspired by the text, not reconstructions of surviving ancient forms.
variants: Yuk Ro Cho Dan to Yuk Dan

meaning: Pseudonym of the philosopher Yi I (1536-1584), the 'Confucius of Korea'; the 38 movements refer to his birthplace on the 38th degree of latitude and the diagram represents 'scholar'.
name: Yul-Gok
note: Fifth Chang Hon pattern, honouring the neo-Confucian scholar Yi I (Yulgok).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and his pattern team

era: Wanshu 17th-19th century tradition; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Flight of the swallow', from the darting, rising and dropping movements; the alternate Korean name Wang Shu preserves the older Okinawan title Wanshu, said to honour the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (1683).
name: Yun Bi
note: Reached Korea as Shotokan's Enpi (Funakoshi's rename of Wanshu); Tang Soo Do lineages use both Yun Bi and Wang Shu for essentially the same hyung. The Wang Ji origin story is tradition, not documented history.
origin_person: Traditionally linked to the envoy Wang Ji; Tomari-te transmission
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

era: 1980s (style founded 1980; kata published in Fighting Karate, 1985)
meaning: Series names are functional Japanese: beginner's forms, basic forms, sparring forms, throwing forms and real-fight forms; together they encode Sabaki, the repositioning method of moving off-line to the opponent's blind side.
name: Ashihara kata series
note: Ashihara discarded the traditional Okinawan-Japanese kata canon of his Kyokushin upbringing entirely and composed these modern series so that every movement maps directly onto full-contact fighting at short, middle and long range, performable solo or with a partner. They are documented as kata by the style's own organisations and publications.

meaning: Named by grade rather than image: graded sequences expressing Enshin's circle-centre (enshin) principle, using Sabaki to convert an opponent's force by moving to the blind spot and unbalancing.
name: Enshin kata series
note: Ninomiya, Ashihara's former student, built Enshin's belt-graded kata on the same Sabaki logic as the Ashihara series rather than on classical forms; no kata named Junro is documented in Enshin (that name belongs to Tetsuhiko Asai's Shotokan series). The forms are documented in Enshin organisational material and style references.

meaning: 'Reclining dragon': a great man who remains humble and unseen, like a dragon lying at rest; in Japanese tradition the garyu is a hidden genius who does not flaunt his power.
name: Garyu
note: The only advanced Kyokushin kata with no Okinawan antecedent, created by Oyama and named after his pen name Garyu, itself the Japanese reading of the characters for Il Loong, the Korean village of his birth. It showcases Kyokushin-specific fighting technique including sacrifice moves and low sweeps.

meaning: 'Peaceful and safe, numbers one to five': Kyokushin retains Itosu's original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's rename Heian.
name: Pinan sono ichi-go
note: Oyama restructured the five Pinan with Kyokushin stances, circular blocks and Goju flavouring, and added ura versions performed with spinning turns, credited to him as a training method for balance and close fighting. The retention of the name Pinan signals Kyokushin's dual Shotokan-Goju parentage.
origin_person: Anko Itosu (originals); Kyokushin adaptation by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; adapted in Tokyo, Japan

era: Qing-era China and Meiji Okinawa; in Kyokushin from the 1950s
meaning: 'Three battles': the struggle to unify mind, body and technique (or mind, body and spirit) through tension, rooted stepping and ibuki breathing.
name: Sanchin (Kyokushin)
note: Oyama absorbed Sanchin through his Goju-ryu training under So Nei Chu (of the Gogen Yamaguchi line) and made it Kyokushin's core conditioning kata, following Miyagi's closed-fist form. The same Goju channel supplied Kyokushin's Gekisai, Saiha (Saifa), Seienchin, Seipai and Tensho.
origin_person: Fujian Chinese lineage via Kanryo Higaonna; closed-fist version by Chojun Miyagi; brought into Kyokushin by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Fuzhou, China / Naha, Okinawa; Kyokushin version Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': an alternative Japanese reading of the same characters as Gojushiho, the number 54 carrying Buddhist significance (half of 108, the number of worldly desires).
name: Sushiho
note: Oyama's rendering of Gojushiho (the old Useshi), reached via its Shotokan transmission and modified to Kyokushin body mechanics; the reading Sushiho distinguishes it from Shotokan's Gojushiho Dai and Sho. It sits among the highest kata of the Kyokushin canon.
origin_person: Shuri-te lineage (Matsumura/Itosu line); Kyokushin version by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; adapted in Tokyo, Japan

meaning: 'Grand ultimate, numbers one to three': the Kyokushin rendering of Funakoshi's Taikyoku, taught as the gateway to the style's kata canon.
name: Taikyoku sono ichi-san
note: Oyama, a direct student of Funakoshi, carried the Taikyoku into Kyokushin with modified stances and fighting emphasis, later adding ura (spinning) versions and the Sokugi (kicking) Taikyoku set unique to the Kyokushin lineage. They remain the first kata across nearly all Kyokushin offshoots.
origin_person: adapted by Mas Oyama from the Shotokan Taikyoku of Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi

meaning: 'Rotating palms' (or 'revolving hands'): soft circular open-hand movements over a Sanchin base, the yin counterpart to Sanchin's hardness.
name: Tensho (Kyokushin)
note: Oyama prized Tensho above all forms, writing that it was 'the most indispensable of the advanced kata' and the distillation of karate's hard-soft principle; it entered Kyokushin directly from his Goju-ryu training. The kata is Miyagi's composition, so its presence in Kyokushin is transmission, not creation.
origin_person: Chojun Miyagi (created 1921, drawing on the Chinese Rokkishu); brought into Kyokushin by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa; Kyokushin version Tokyo, Japan

era: mid-20th century (Seigokan founded 1945); in Kyokushin by the 1960s-70s
meaning: 'Kata of punches' (or 'of thrusts'): a form built almost entirely from stepping punches, symbolising fortune arriving with each decisive strike in Kyokushin lore.
name: Tsuki no Kata
note: Created by Seigo Tada as Kihon Tsuki no kata, one of two Seigokan founder-kata; how it entered Kyokushin is not securely documented, and the common attribution to Tadashi Nakamura as creator is an error, though he is plausibly the conduit given his Goju background (speculative, flagged as such in Kyokushin histories). [Verifier: Creator confirmed: Seigo Tada of Seigokan Goju-ryu (where it is Kihon
origin_person: Seigo Tada, founder of Seigokan Goju-ryu

meaning: Usually written with characters read as 'safe three' and glossed in Kyokushin as 'to keep pure', striving to maintain integrity of principle under pressure; the etymology is debated.
name: Yantsu
note: The most origin-disputed kata in Kyokushin: style histories suggest descent from Ansan (Hansan) preserved in Motobu-ha Shito-ryu, modified by Oyama, but no primary documentation settles the question, so all accounts should be treated as provisional. It appears in no mainstream Okinawan syllabus outside these lines.
origin_person: uncertain; plausibly adapted by Mas Oyama from the kata Ansan/Hansan of Motobu-ha Shito-ryu

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: Meaning uncertain: the characters can be read as 'peace in the south' and are often linked to Annan (a historical name for Vietnam) or to a Chinese place or personal name. Ryuei-ryu's most famous kata, noted for lateral evasion and techniques repeated no more than twice.
name: Anan
note: Kept secret within the Nakaima family for four generations until Kenko Nakaima opened Ryuei-ryu in 1971; Teruo Hayashi carried it into Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu, and Tsuguo Sakumoto's WUKO world titles (1984-1988) made it a dominant competition kata. The family origin story (Norisato's c. 7 years with Ryu Ryu Ko in Fuzhou) is tradition with limited external corroboration.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

era: imported in the 4th family generation (Kaho Kojo, 1849-1925)
meaning: Earth (chi) form: third elemental kata of Kojo-ryu, grounding the zodiac kamae-te method in low, rooted positions.
name: Chikan
note: Completes the heaven-void-earth set attributed to Kaho Kojo's importation from Fuzhou; like all Kojo-ryu material its history rests on family tradition rather than external records.
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Kume village, Naha

meaning: Attack and smash, number one. A deliberately simple popularisation kata: direct blocks, lunging punches and kicks designed to teach schoolchildren and beginners quickly.
name: Gekisai dai ichi
note: Created in 1940 for the karate promotion committee convened under Okinawa governor Hayakawa Gen, as Naha-te's contribution to a common beginner syllabus alongside Shoshin Nagamine's Fukyugata ichi. Later absorbed into Kyokushin as Gekisai dai.

meaning: Attack and smash, number two. Extends Gekisai dai ichi with open-hand techniques, mawashi-uke and neko-ashi-dachi, introducing the softer receiving methods characteristic of Goju-ryu.
name: Gekisai dai ni
note: Companion kata to Gekisai dai ichi from the same 1940 popularisation programme; the pair are Miyagi's last compositions and the standard entry point of the modern Goju curriculum.

era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
meaning: White crane. Third and highest animal kata of Kojo-ryu, expressing evasive footwork and wing-like simultaneous deflection and strike.
name: Hakkaku
note: Completes the tiger-dragon-crane triad; extended Kojo-ryu lists also record Hafa, Nepai, Nunfa, Paichu and other Fujian-named forms, consistent with the family's Kume-village Chinese heritage but thinly documented. Kojo-ryu is grouped here with Naha-te as Kuninda-di for cladogram purposes. [Verifier: Exists; 'white crane', highest animal kata, correct in meaning and character. Same caveat: the Koj
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
variants: Hakkaku (white crane); distinct from the Matayoshi/Gokenki Hakkaku-Hakucho crane kata of the same name

era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
meaning: White tiger. First of Kojo-ryu's three advanced animal kata (tiger, dragon, crane), expressing hard crushing and clawing method.
name: Hakko
note: The three 'white beast' kata are the core of the family style; the attribution to the early Kojo generations (and their teacher-relations with Fuzhou masters such as Wai Shin Zan) is folklore preserved by the family, not independently documented. [Verifier: The kata exists and 'white tiger' is correct; Hakko, Hakuryu and Hakkaku are confirmed as Kojo-ryu's advanced animal triad. However, published
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China

era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
meaning: White dragon. Second animal kata of Kojo-ryu, expressing soft, coiling, whipping method between the tiger's hardness and the crane's lightness.
name: Hakuryu
note: Preserved through the Kojo family line (Isei, Taitei, Kaho, Saikyo, Kafu, Shigeru Kojo) and a handful of outside students; the pre-Okinawan history is family folklore. [Verifier: Exists; 'white dragon', second animal kata, correct. Same attribution caveat as Hakko: sources point to Kojo Taitei introducing the animal triad, so the 18th-century Kojo Uekata lineage claim is unverifiable tradition.]
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: Black tiger. Sister kata to Paiku expressing the darker, heavier side of Fujian tiger boxing; the two share much material and are distinguished by rhythm and emphasis.
name: Heiku
note: Nakaima family transmission opened to the public in 1971; entered mainstream competition through Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu and Sakumoto's students. Kanji renderings vary across sources as the names are phonetic Fujian dialect.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

era: imported in the 4th family generation (Kaho Kojo, 1849-1925)
meaning: Void or sky (ku) form: second of the three elemental kata of Kojo-ryu, continuing the zodiac kamae-te system at intermediate level.
name: Kukan
note: Middle kata of the heaven-void-earth trio said to have been brought from the Kojo family dojo in Fuzhou by Kaho Kojo; preserved only in the nearly extinct Kojo-ryu line (Kafu Kojo, Shigeru Kojo, Hayashi Shingo).
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Kume village, Naha

meaning: Conventionally 'holding on long and striking suddenly' (the kanji are phonetic). The most fluid of the classical Goju kata, alternating slow sticky-hand control with explosive release; strong White Crane character.
name: Kururunfa
note: Goju tradition ascribes it to Higaonna via Ryu Ryu Ko, but it is absent from To'on-ryu and its documented history before Miyagi is thin; scholars regard the pre-Okinawan origin as unverified.

meaning: Twenty-eight (steps). A Fujian Whooping/White Crane form built on fast whipping strikes and crane-wing deflections; in Okinawa it is the signature legacy of the Chinese tea merchant Gokenki.
name: Nepai
note: Kyoda Juhatsu learned Nepai directly from Gokenki and fixed it in the To'on-ryu curriculum; Kenwa Mabuni reworked the same material as Nipaipo in Shito-ryu. A Nepai also appears in extended Kojo-ryu kata lists, consistent with the family's Kume-village White Crane contacts.
variants: Nipaipo (二十八歩, Mabuni's Shito-ryu adaptation)

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: Twenty-four (steps/hands). The Ryuei-ryu version of a Fuzhou form also transmitted separately by Aragaki Seisho (whence Shito-ryu's Niseishi and Shotokan's Nijushiho).
name: Niseishi (Ryuei-ryu)
note: Listed in the Ryuei-ryu (Ryuho-kai) curriculum alongside Sanchin, Seisan and Sanseiru; its coexistence with Seisho Arakaki's independent Niseishi line supports a shared Fuzhou source pool rather than a single Okinawan origin.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
variants: cognate with Aragaki Niseishi / Nijushiho but a distinct transmission

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: Meaning and kanji uncertain (phonetic Fujian name; sometimes glossed as 'king's crown' or a personal name in style folklore). Alternates heavy rooted techniques with sudden turns and double-hand strikes.
name: Ohan
note: Nakaima family kata made public in 1971; its extended version Ohan Dai became globally visible when Kiyou Shimizu and other Shito-ryu-trained competitors performed it at WKF finals and the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: Meaning and kanji uncertain (a phonetic Fujian-dialect name). An extremely fast, dynamic kata teaching lateral evasion and moving into the opponent with difficult combinations.
name: Pachu
note: One of the six kata unique to the Nakaima family line (Anan, Paiku, Heiku, Pachu, Ohan, Paiho), secret until 1971 and now on the WKF kata list; the untranslatable name reflects oral Fuzhou transmission.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
variants: Pachu Dai/Sho in some competition listings

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: White phoenix (or white crane). A characteristic White Crane kata: light footwork, wing-like simultaneous deflection and strike; its opening closely parallels Hakkaku, Hakucho and other Okinawan crane forms from the Gokenki milieu.
name: Paiho
note: The most explicitly crane-styled of the Nakaima family kata, kept within the family until Kenko Nakaima's 1971 opening of the school; rarely seen outside Ryuei-ryu organisations.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
meaning: White tiger. Embodies Fujian tiger-boxing method within the Nakaima family curriculum: clawing hands, pouncing shifts and hard direct power; paired conceptually with Heiku (black tiger).
name: Paiku
note: Part of the Nakaima family transmission from Ryu Ryu Ko, made public by Kenko Nakaima in 1971 and adopted into Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu and WKF competition lists; very similar in structure to Heiku.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

meaning: Smash and tear (destroy and defeat). Teaches escaping from grabs at close quarters with whipping strikes, hammer-fists and tearing hand actions.
name: Saifa
note: Traditionally credited to Higaonna's Fuzhou study under Ryu Ryu Ko, but its absence from Kyoda Juhatsu's To'on-ryu (which preserves only Sanchin, Sesan, Sanseru and Pechurin from Higaonna) leads scholars such as Mario McKenna to suggest Miyagi introduced it from his own Chinese research; treat the Higaonna attribution as tradition rather than documented fact.

era: Qing-era China; taught in Naha from c. 1880s
meaning: Three battles (or conflicts): the struggle to unify mind, body and breath. The foundational conditioning kata of all Naha-lineage karate, built on rooted stance, dynamic tension and controlled breathing.
name: Sanchin
note: Two independent transmissions from Fuzhou: Higaonna brought a version credited to Ryu Ryu Ko (said to have been performed with open hands, which Higaonna, or by some accounts Miyagi, closed into fists; Miyagi also removed the turns and slowed the breathing, creating the Goju version), while Kanbun Uechi brought Zhou Zihe's Pangai-noon version, which keeps open-hand nukite strikes and faster, unforced breathing. The identification of Ryu Ryu Ko with the Whooping Crane master Xie Zongxiang is plausible but disputed scholarship.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted the Higaonna line; ultimate creator unknown, Fujian tradition)

meaning: Thirty-six (hands). The number is usually explained through Buddhist/Chinese numerology (6 x 6: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, spirit; colour, voice, taste, smell, touch, justice). Features low kicks, joint attacks and double-hand techniques.
name: Sanseiru
note: One of the four kata reliably traceable to Higaonna (preserved in both Goju-ryu and To'on-ryu). The Nakaima family's Ryuei-ryu preserves its own Sanseiru from the same Ryu Ryu Ko source, and Uechi-ryu's Sanseiryu (listed separately) is a distinct Pangai-noon form sharing only the name.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)

meaning: Usually rendered as 'to control and pull into battle' (the kanji are a phonetic gloss); sometimes 'calm within the storm'. A kick-free kata of grappling, unbalancing and pulling techniques performed largely in shiko-dachi.
name: Seiyunchin
note: Attributed by Goju tradition to Higaonna's Naha-te, though like Saifa it is absent from To'on-ryu, so a Miyagi-era introduction is possible. Entered Kyokushin (as Seienchin) via the Goju line, and Isshin-ryu (as Seiunchin) through Tatsuo Shimabuku's study under Miyagi.

meaning: Eighteen (hands), conventionally 6 x 3 in Buddhist numerology (the six senses in three aspects). An advanced kata of angular evasion, hidden strikes and off-line body shifting.
name: Sepai
note: Attributed by tradition to Higaonna's Fuzhou study; not preserved in To'on-ryu, so the same caveat as Saifa applies. Practised in Kyokushin as Seipai via the Goju-kai line.

meaning: Thirteen (hands), variously explained as thirteen techniques or 13 as an auspicious number. The Naha version emphasises close-range hard-soft striking, low kicks and heavy rooted stepping.
name: Sesan
note: Seisan is arguably the most widely distributed kata name in karate; this entry covers the Naha transmission preserved in Goju-ryu, To'on-ryu (one of Kyoda's four Higaonna kata) and Ryuei-ryu. The Uechi and Shuri/Tomari Seisan are separate transmissions. [Verifier: Kata, meaning ('thirteen') and Naha character correct. The introduced_by set is defensible (Kyoda's To'on-ryu preserves Higaonna's Sesa
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
variants: Hangetsu and Shuri Seisan are cognate but distinct Shuri/Tomari forms
